summary: Defines a new sub-option of the CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) DHCP option for conveying the network addresses of Key Distribution Center (KDC) servers. This lets cable devices learn where to find the servers that handle Kerberos-style key distribution. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A new gadget needs to know where the key-handing office is. This adds a spot in the setup message that tells it the office's address.

questions: how do cable devices find a kdc
what is the kdc server address sub-option
what is dhcp ccc option sub-option 10
how does a cablehome gateway find its kdc
what length can the kdc sub-option have
subtitle: A small DHCP sub-option that tells a cable device the IPv4 addresses of its Kerberos key servers.

tldr.problem: CableHome residential gateways that use Kerberos need to know where the Key Distribution Center (KDC) is, but they cannot rely on a DNS lookup of the Kerberos realm name to find it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines sub-option 10 of the CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) DHCP option. It carries one or more IPv4 addresses of KDC servers, listed in decreasing order of priority.
tldr.outcome: A configured device learns its KDC addresses straight from DHCP. The RFC adds no security of its own and relies on DHCP, the cable network design and Kerberos authentication.

today: RFC 3634 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the definition of the KDC Server Address sub-option (code 10) of the CCC option.

sections.title: Why a KDC Address Is Needed
sections.content:
CableHome-compliant residential gateways may use Kerberos for authentication. That is the first step in setting up a secure SNMPv3 link between the Portal Service (PS) element in the gateway and the SNMP entity in the cable operator's data network. To start Kerberos, the device must know the network address of a Key Distribution Center (KDC) server in the operator's network.

The RFC meets this need with a new sub-option of the CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) DHCP option. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: A device cannot ask the key office for help if it does not know the office's address. The setup message now includes that address.

sections.title: Why DNS Is Not Used
sections.content:
The devices in the CableHome specifications are unlike the class of devices in RFC 3495, which perform a DNS lookup of the Kerberos realm name to find the KDC server address. For these gateways the RFC instead encodes the address directly, giving an identifier for the network address of each of one or more KDC servers with which the device exchanges security information.

The sub-option is meant for CableLabs client devices only, and the CCC option itself is defined in RFC 3495.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets look up the office's address in a phone book. These gadgets are simply handed the address when they are set up.

sections.title: The KDC Server Address Sub-option
sections.content:
The sub-option follows the format of an IPv4 address. It starts with the sub-option code 10 and a length field n, followed by one or more four-octet addresses.

  • The minimum length is 4 octets, and the length MUST always be a multiple of 4.
  • If several KDC servers are listed, they MUST be listed in decreasing order of priority.

The RFC says the CableHome specifications will specify the KDC network address encoding as a sub-option of the CCC option code.
sections.eli5: It is a list of addresses, four bytes each, with the best choice first. A length number says how long the list is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC relies on DHCP for authentication and security and does not provide more than DHCP does. It points to section 7 of the DHCP specification and to Authentication for DHCP Messages (RFC 3118) for the attacks DHCP is exposed to.

The CCC option can misdirect traffic by giving a device incorrect addresses or Kerberos realm names. The RFC names three threats: a denial of service from simply invalid addresses, a man-in-the-middle attack by pointing devices at a snooper, and a malicious service provider stealing customers by altering the Kerberos realm designation.

It lists several mitigations:

  • The CMTS is explicitly configured with the DHCP servers that requests are forwarded to, and a correctly configured CMTS only allows downstream traffic from specific IP addresses or ranges.
  • A device that reaches a spoofed KDC must still present valid certificates, although the computational cost of certificate validation could itself be a DoS opportunity.
  • Service providers can put the KDCs on a separate subnetwork or behind a firewall that only allows the connections needed for provisioning.
  • Kerberos requires mutual client-server authentication, so a replaced KDC address is unlikely to point to a valid provider's KDC and authentication will fail.

A malicious but certificate-enabled service provider is treated as an administrative matter between the access provider and the service provider.
sections.eli5: Someone could give the gadget a wrong address. But the network only lets in trusted traffic, and the real key office checks who is asking, so a fake office would fail the check.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The KDC Server Address sub-option is a sub-option of the CCC option described in RFC 3495. IANA has assigned and registered sub-option code 10 of the CCC option to it.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers now reserves number 10 for this address slot, so nobody else uses it.

fields.name: SubOpt
fields.desc: Sub-option code of the KDC Server Address sub-option.

fields.name: Len
fields.desc: Length of the addresses, a multiple of 4 and at least 4.

fields.name: Address 1
fields.desc: First KDC server, an IPv4 address (a1 to a4). Further addresses follow in decreasing priority.
